identity.name: Libyan Arab Republic (Libyan Arab Jamahiriya)
native_names: الجماهيرية العربية الليبية الشعبية الاشتراكية العظمى (al-Jamāhīriyya al-ʿArabiyya al-Lībiyya ash-Shaʿbiyya al-Ishtirākiyya al-ʿUẓmā)

identity.wikipedia: History of Libya under Muammar Gaddafi

land.text: all of Libya: Gaddafi 'seized control of the government and in a stroke abolished the Libyan monarchy' on 1 September 1969

predecessors.note: Cliopatria's Kingdom row ends 1968 and this row begins 1969 with the same outline.

land.text: all of Libya, the same outline

successors.note: A row boundary, not a change of state: the page says Libya was governed by the General National Congress at the beginning of 2014; Cliopatria's State of Libya row begins 2014.

capitals.name: Tripoli
capitals.note: Infobox of the Libya page: Tripoli, 32°52′N 13°11′E. The Gaddafi page adds that in September 2011 Gaddafi 'declared [Sirte] the new capital of Libya'; the page does not say when this ended, so no Sirte entry is drawn.

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 1.614 M km2 is the modern Libyan outline; the Libya infobox gives 1,759,541 km2 (ratio 0.92, within the factor of two). The coup was on 1 September 1969, so January-August 1969 belongs to the kingdom (Cliopatria's Kingdom row ends 1968). The shape excludes the Aouzou Strip (114,000 km2 per the Aouzou Strip page), which Libya occupied from 1973: that is carried by an occupation event, not by the shape.

1,614,070 km2 against 1,614,019 km2 for 1969-1972: the 51 km2 difference is a one-cell artefact. The page says Libya 'occupied [the Aouzou Strip] in 1973'; the strip is not in the shape and is drawn by the occupation event of 1973.

Same outline as 1969 (1,614,019 km2). The Jamahiriya (proclaimed 2 March 1977) changed the name, not the territory; the 1994 withdrawal from the Aouzou Strip leaves the shape unchanged because the strip was never in it.

Same outline to 2013. In 2011 the east (Benghazi, Bayda) slipped from Tripoli's control from 18-19 February to the National Transitional Council; the shape stays the de jure state and the rebel zone is carried by contest events (ledger 2011). The row ends 2013 and Cliopatria's State of Libya begins 2014, a boundary the pages opened do not explain.

region.text: the whole of Libya, taken over from the kingdom

ledger.note: 1 September 1969: Gaddafi's coup abolishes the monarchy and proclaims the Libyan Arab Republic. The coup plotters 'seized control of the government and in a stroke abolished the Libyan monarchy'; the Revolutionary Command Council declared 'a free and sovereign state called the Libyan Arab Republic'.

region.text: the Aouzou Strip, 'an area of 114,000 km2' in northern Chad

ledger.note: 1973: Libya occupies and annexes the Aouzou Strip of northern Chad. 'Hence, in 1973, Libya proceeded to occupy and annex the mineral-rich area without any Chadian resistance'; the strip is 'an area of 114,000 km2' and the page ties the move to an April 1972 agreement between Gaddafi and Tombalbaye. Chad records the matching event.

2 March 1977: the General People's Congress proclaims the Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya. The country keeps its outline and its ruler; it was 'renamed again in 1986' as the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya.

region.text: northern Chad around Faya-Largeau, taken 18 February 1978 by rebels with Libyan armour and air support

ledger.note: February 1978: Libyan-backed rebels take Faya-Largeau and the north of Chad. Faya-Largeau 'fell on 18 February 1978 after sharp fighting' to rebels backed by Libyan armour, artillery and air support; the page dates the conflict from 29 January 1978. The zone (Borkou, Ennedi, Tibesti, the old BET) is the researcher's reading of the north; the page names the town.

region.text: the Chadian capital, which fell on 16 December 1980

ledger.note: 16 December 1980: the Libyan-backed attack takes N'Djamena. 'An attack started on 6 December 1980' and brought 'the fall of the capital on 16 December'; Libyan forces then stayed in Chad until the next November. The page names the capital, not the extent of the Libyan hold, so the region is a 200 km circle round it.

region.text: northern Chad, left by Libyan forces by 16 November 1981

ledger.note: 16 November 1981: Libyan forces leave Chad proper. 'by 16 November all Libyan forces had left Chad', after Chad's demand of 29 October 1981; the Aouzou Strip stays occupied.

region.text: the Chadian capital and its surroundings, left by Libyan forces by 16 November 1981

ledger.note: 16 November 1981: the Libyan occupation of the Chadian capital ends with the withdrawal of all Libyan forces from Chad proper.

region.text: northern Chad, the land north of the French 'Red Line' held by Libya and its Chadian allies

ledger.note: June 1983: Libya returns to northern Chad. Faya-Largeau 'fell on 25 June 1983' after a Libyan-backed GUNT offensive; the French 'Red Line' along the 15th parallel (raised to the 16th after 24 January 1984) left 'Libya maintaining control of all the territory north of the Red Line'. The zone is the researcher's reading of the land north of the line.
1986: the Jamahiriya takes its final name. 'The country was renamed again in 1986 as the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya.' No change of territory.

region.text: northern Chad, the zone fought over from 1978 to the 11 September 1987 ceasefire

ledger.note: 11 September 1987: an OAU-brokered ceasefire ends the Toyota War. Habre began his reconquest on 2 January 1987 at Fada, B'ir Kora and Ouadi Doum followed in March, and 'Aouzou fell in August to the FANT, only to be repelled by an overwhelming Libyan counter-offensive'. Libya keeps the Aouzou Strip, so that stays in the occupation event until 1994.

region.text: the Aouzou Strip, returned to Chad after the ICJ judgement of 3 February 1994

ledger.note: May 1994: Libya leaves the Aouzou Strip. The ICJ ruled for Chad 16 to 1 on 3 February 1994; 'the withdrawal of Libyan troops from the Strip began on 15 April and was completed by 10 May', with the formal transfer on 30 May. The Aouzou Strip page adds that Security Council resolutions 915 and 926 set up and wound up the observer group.

region.text: Benghazi and Bayda, from which the security forces withdrew on 18-19 February 2011

ledger.note: 18 February 2011: the east slips from Tripoli's control. 'On 18 February, police and army personnel later withdrew from Benghazi after being overwhelmed by protesters' and the army left Bayda; the National Transitional Council was formed on 27 February. The page names the cities, not a front line, so the zone is Cyrenaica by the researcher's reading; the war widened to Misrata and the west before Tripoli fell (the page: final assault on Bab al-Azizia on 24 August, 28 August 2011 for the fall of Tripoli).

20 October 2011: Sirte falls and the Jamahiriya ends. The page: the fall of Sirte on 20 October 2011 'marked the end of the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya'; Gaddafi was captured and killed that day. The state carries on as 'Libya' under the National Transitional Council, which the UN recognised as the legal representative of Libya on 16 September 2011 (First Libyan Civil War page).

region.text: the whole country, the zone the NTC and the Gaddafi regime fought over from February to October 2011

ledger.note: 23 October 2011: the National Transitional Council declares 'the liberation of Libya' and the official end of the war. The war ran from 15 February to 23 October 2011 with the result 'Complete overthrow and collapse of the Gaddafi regime'.

region.text: all of Libya, passing unchanged to the State of Libya row of 2014

ledger.note: 2013: Cliopatria's Libyan Arab Republic row ends and its State of Libya row begins in 2014. The page does not date a break in the state: 'At the beginning of 2014, Libya was governed by the General National Congress' (elected 7 July 2012, which received power from the NTC on 8 August 2012 per the Libya page), which 'failed to stand down at the end of its electoral mandate in January 2014'. Treated as the row boundary; land passes to the State of Libya.

wars.name: Chadian-Libyan conflict

zones.text: northern Chad (Borkou, Ennedi, Tibesti), the zone fought over
the Aouzou Strip, occupied by Libya from 1973 to 1994

wars.outcome: Chadian and French victory in the infobox: Libya was pushed out of Chad proper by November 1981, returned in 1983 and was beaten in the 1987 Toyota War (ceasefire 11 September 1987), but kept the Aouzou Strip until the ICJ judgement of 3 February 1994 and the withdrawal of April-May 1994.
wars.note: Infobox 'Date: 29 January 1978 - 11 September 1987'. The occupation of the Aouzou Strip began in 1973, before the page's dates (Aouzou Strip page).

wars.name: Libyan-Egyptian War
wars.outcome: Border gun battles from 21 July 1977 ended by a ceasefire on 24 July 1977 mediated by Algeria and Arafat; no territory changed hands.
wars.note: The page gives no zone and no change of the frontier.

wars.name: First Libyan Civil War

zones.text: the east, where the security forces withdrew from Benghazi and Bayda on 18-19 February 2011

wars.outcome: 'Libyan opposition/NATO victory - Complete overthrow and collapse of the Gaddafi regime': Tripoli fell in August, Gaddafi was killed at Sirte on 20 October and the NTC declared the liberation of Libya on 23 October 2011.
wars.note: Infobox 'Date: 15 February 2011 - 23 October 2011'. The page does not give a front line, so only Cyrenaica is named as the contested zone.

certainty.note: Libya's modern frontier is a treaty frontier (the Aouzou Strip page mentions the 1899, 1935 and 1955 agreements); the exception is the southern frontier with Chad, where Libya occupied the Aouzou Strip from 1973 against the 1955 treaty line, so the strip and the northern Chad zones are soft.
The Chad frontier is fixed by the ICJ judgement of 3 February 1994 ('16 to 1' for Chad); in 2011 the line between regime and rebels was a moving front the pages do not draw.

notes: Five Cliopatria-based decisions and gaps. (1) THE ROW: the Libyan Arab Republic row (1969-2013) is one continuous state under Gaddafi and then the NTC, renamed in 1977, 1986 and 2011; it is drawn as one dossier, and Cliopatria's State of Libya (2014-2024, another group's slug 'state-of-libya', not yet written when this was done) continues the same outline, so the split at 2013/2014 is a row boundary and not a change of state; the colour agent may wish to keep one colour from the Kingdom of Libya (1951) to 2024. The end year 2013 follows Cliopatria; the pages opened date no break in the state. (2) THE SHAPE is modern Libya (1.614 M km2) in all four keyframes; they differ by one-cell artefacts. The Aouzou Strip is outside it and is drawn as an occupation, 1973-1994, with the matching events in the republic-of-chad dossier (same region name 'Aouzou Strip', a name the gazetteer lacks). (3) The Chadian-Libyan events (1978-81, 1983-87, N'Djamena 1980-81) mirror the contest and occupation events of republic-of-chad; the zones there and here use the same three Chadian provinces (Borkou, Ennedi, Tibesti) as an approximation of the old BET prefecture, and the Libyan hold of N'Djamena is a 200 km circle that is the researcher's reading. The 1980 Libyan-supported attack, the 1983 Red Line and the 1987 Aouzou swing are dated from the Chadian-Libyan conflict page; the Aouzou Strip page also says Chadian forces 'were able to force the Libyans to temporarily retreat from part of the Strip' in 1987. (4) NOT DRAWN, page silent or no territory: the 1972 Federation of Arab Republics with Egypt and Syria ('effectively dormant after 1973'; an association, never territory); the abandonment of the British bases at El Adem and Tobruk on 27 March 1970 and of Wheelus Air Base on 11 June 1970 (a few square kilometres); the 1977 clashes with Egypt (war entry, no zone); the Gulf of Sirte naval clashes of 19 August 1981, 23 March 1986 and 4 January 1989 (the page gives no claim line); unification attempts with Egypt and Tunisia (the Gaddafi page dates none; Tunisia is not mentioned). (5) 2011: the NTC held the east from February and the Nafusa Mountains and Misrata later, but the First Libyan Civil War page gives no front lines, so the only contest zone is Cyrenaica from 18 February; a gap-filler should open 'Timeline of the 2011 Libyan civil war' for the fall of Misrata, the Nafusa front and Tripoli (24-28 August). The 2012-2013 years (General National Congress elected 7 July 2012, handover 8 August 2012) are on the Libya page only, and any territorial contest of 2012-2013 is on no page opened: History_of_Libya_since_2011 could not be loaded (url_not_found twice) and the Libya page gives only the election and the handover. FAILED PAGES: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chadian%E2%80%93Libyan_conflict and the en-dash form (url_not_found; the hyphen form loaded), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Libya_since_2011 (url_not_found, tried twice). Gazetteer names needed: 'Aouzou Strip' (region, the northern part of Chad's Tibesti, 114,000 km2). Native names are as the English Wikipedia infobox spells them; no ruler strip is given because the pages opened list no rulers after Gaddafi's death.
